<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The natural gas and
oil business involves many operating risks that can cause substantial losses or
hinder marketing efforts.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Numerous risks
affect the Company&#146;s drilling activities, including the risk of drilling
non-productive wells or dry holes. The cost of drilling, completing and
operating wells and of installing production facilities and pipelines is often
uncertain. Also, the Company&#146;s drilling operations could diminish or cease
because of any of the following:</font></p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>title
problems;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>weather
conditions;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>fires;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>explosions;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>blow-outs
and surface cratering;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>uncontrollable
flows of underground natural gas, oil and formation water;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>natural
disasters;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>pipe
or cement failures;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>casing
collapses;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>embedded
oilfield drilling and service tools;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>abnormally
pressured formations;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>environmental
hazards such as natural gas leaks, oil spills, pipeline ruptures and discharges
of toxic gases;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>noncompliance
with governmental requirements; or</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>shortages
or delays in the delivery or availability of material, equipment or fabrication
yards.</p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Offshore operations are also subject to a variety of
operating risks related to the marine environment, such as capsizing,
collisions and damage or loss from hurricanes or other adverse weather
conditions. These hazards may interrupt production and can cause substantial
losses to the Company due to injury or loss of life, severe damage to
facilities, or pollution or other environmental damage. As a result, the
Company could incur substantial liabilities that could reduce or eliminate the
funds available for exploration, development or leasehold acquisitions.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Moreover, effective
marketing of the Company&#146;s natural gas production depends on a number of
factors, such as the following:</font></p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>existing
market supply of and demand for natural gas;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>the
proximity of the Company&#146;s reserves to pipelines;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>the
available capacity of such pipelines; and</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>government
regulations.</p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The marketing of oil and
natural gas production similarly depends on the availability of pipelines and
other transportation, processing and refining facilities, and the existence of
adequate markets. As a result, even if hydrocarbons are discovered in commercial
quantities, a substantial period of time may elapse before commercial
production commences. If pipeline facilities in an area are insufficient, the
Company </font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">may have
to wait for the construction or expansion of pipeline capacity before the
Company can market production from that area.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company may not
be able to obtain sufficient drilling equipment and experienced personnel to
conduct its operations.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In periods of increased
drilling activity resulting from high commodity prices, demand exceeds
availability for drilling rigs, drilling vessels, supply boats and personnel
experienced in the oil and gas industry in general, and the offshore oil and
gas industry in particular. This may lead to difficulty and delays in
consistently obtaining services and equipment from vendors, obtaining drilling
rigs and other equipment at favorable rates, and scheduling equipment
fabrication at factories and fabrication yards. This, in turn, may lead to
projects being delayed or experiencing increased costs.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s foreign operations subject it to
additional risks.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 4.5pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
Company&#146;s ownership and operations in Canada, New Zealand, Vietnam and any
other foreign areas where it does business are subject to the various risks
inherent in foreign operations. These risks may include the following:</font></p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 4.5pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>currency
restrictions and exchange rate fluctuations;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 4.5pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>risks
of increases in taxes and governmental royalties and renegotiation of contracts
with governmental entities; and</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 4.5pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>changes
in laws and policies governing operations of foreign-based companies.</p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">United States laws and policies on foreign trade,
taxation and investment may also adversely affect the Company&#146;s international
operations. In addition, if a dispute arises from foreign operations, foreign
courts may have exclusive jurisdiction over the dispute, or the Company may not
be able to subject foreign persons to the jurisdiction of United States courts.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10.5pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Local laws and customs in
many countries differ significantly from those in the United States. In many
foreign countries, particularly in those with developing economies like
Vietnam, it is common to engage in business practices that are prohibited by
United States regulations applicable to the Company. The U.S. Foreign Corrupt
Practices Act prohibits corporations and individuals, including the Company and
its employees, from engaging in certain activities to obtain or retain business
or to influence a person working in an official capacity. Although the Company
has implemented policies and procedures designed to ensure compliance with
these laws, there can be no assurance that all of the Company&#146;s employees,
contractors and agents, including those based in or from countries where
practices which violate such United States laws may be customary, will not take
actions in violation of the Company&#146;s policies. Any such violation, even if
prohibited by the Company&#146;s policies, could have a material adverse effect on
the Company&#146;s business. In addition, the Company&#146;s foreign competitors that are
not subject to the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act or similar laws may be
able to secure business or other preferential treatment in such countries by
means that such laws prohibit with respect to the Company.</font></p>

control the activities on properties it does not operate; operators of those
properties may act in ways that are not in the Company&#146;s best interests.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Other companies

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Maintaining

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company must
continually explore for and develop or acquire new oil and natural gas reserves

exploration or acquisition activities. Although the Company has historically
maintained its reserves base primarily through successful exploration and
development operations, its future efforts may not be similarly successful.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s operations are subject to casualty risks
against which it cannot fully insure.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s operations
are subject to inherent casualty risks such as blowouts, fires, explosions,
cratering, uncontrollable flows of oil, natural gas or well fluids, pollution
and other environmental risks, marine hazards and natural disasters. If any
such event occurred, the Company could be subject to substantial financial
losses due to personal injury, property damage, environmental discharge, or
suspension of operations. The impact on the Company of one of these events
could be significant. Although the Company purchases insurance at levels it
believes to be customary for a company of its size in its industry, the Company
is not fully insured against all risks incident to its business. For some
risks, the Company may not obtain insurance if it believes the cost of
available insurance is excessive relative to the risks presented. In addition,
pollution and environmental risks generally are not fully insurable. If a
significant accident or other event occurs and is not fully covered by
insurance, it could adversely affect the Company&#146;s operations and financial
condition. Moreover, there is no assurance that recoveries for insured events
will be sufficient to cover cash flow that the Company would have otherwise
generated from affected properties.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company has substantial capital requirements.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company requires

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company financed a
substantial part of the Northrock acquisition utilizing cash on hand, proceeds

borrowings under its revolving credit facility. In addition, the Company
financed a portion of its acquisition of Latigo utilizing borrowings under its
revolving credit facility. Accordingly, these acquisitions reduce the
availability of those resources for other capital requirements. Moreover, the

ultimately determine the Company&#146;s liquidity and ability to meet anticipated
capital requirements.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Rights to repayment
or acceleration of up to $2.3 billion of the Company&#146;s debt and other payments
would be triggered by a change in a majority of the Board of Directors that is
not approved by incumbent directors.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10.5pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On February 23, 2007, a
shareholder formally notified the Company that it intends to conduct a proxy
contest at the Company&#146;s 2007 annual meeting that would, if successful, result
in a change in a majority of the Board of Directors. As of February&nbsp;28,
2007, the Company had approximately $1.45 billion aggregate principal amount of
senior subordinated notes outstanding and approximately $869 million of
outstanding senior indebtedness, approximately $769 million of which was
outstanding under its revolving credit facility.&#160; If there is a change in a majority of the
Board of Directors not approved by a vote of two-thirds of the incumbent
directors, the indentures governing the notes require the Company to offer to
repurchase all outstanding notes at 101% of their principal amount and to repay
all outstanding senior debt, including the credit facility, prior to
repurchasing the notes (or obtain consent from the lenders allowing for such
repurchase). Although such a change in a majority of the Board of Directors
would not, by itself, constitute an event of default under the credit facility,
failure by the Company to perform its indenture obligations would allow the
lenders under the credit facility to accelerate the credit facility debt.
During 2007, two series of the Company&#146;s notes, representing $800 million in
aggregate principal amount, have generally traded below their principal face
value, and the other two series, representing $650 million in aggregate
principal amount, have generally traded above 101% of their principal amount.
The Company cannot predict the actions its noteholders or lenders may take.
However, the Company believes that holders whose notes were trading below the
repurchase price at the time the rights were triggered would exercise their
repurchase rights. Additionally, the Company believes that lenders under its
credit facility and holders whose notes were trading above the repurchase price
may also exercise their repayment or repurchase rights, as the case may be, to
the extent they expect that the holders whose notes were trading below the
repurchase price would exercise such rights or for other reasons. The Company
does not have sufficient cash available to fund a repurchase of all or a
substantial portion of the senior subordinated notes or to repay all or a
substantial portion of outstanding debt under the credit facility.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10.5pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Defaults under, or the
acceleration of, the notes or credit facility could significantly and adversely
affect the Company&#146;s financial position. If the Company were not able to
refinance the debt, it could be required to sell substantial assets at distress
prices in order to satisfy its obligations or to seek protection under the
federal bankruptcy laws. Any refinancing of the Company&#146;s existing debt with
new debt, if available, would likely involve substantial costs, including the
premium to repurchase notes from existing holders and transaction costs
associated with obtaining new debt. Such new debt may be on less favorable
terms than the Company&#146;s existing debt. Refinancing may also negatively impact
the Company&#146;s strategic alternatives initiative.&#160; </font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company will continue to pursue acquisitions and
dispositions.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company will continue to seek opportunities to
generate value through business combinations, purchases and sales of assets. The
Company examines potential transactions on a regular basis, depending on market
conditions, available opportunities and other factors. In addition, the Company
competes with other companies in pursuing acquisitions, many of which have
greater financial and other resources to acquire attractive companies and
properties. The successful acquisition of oil and gas properties requires an
assessment of several factors, including recoverable reserves, development and
exploratory potential, projected future cash flows that are, in part, based
upon future oil and gas prices, current and projected operating, general and
administrative and other costs, and contingent liabilities associated with the
properties or entities acquired, including potential environmental and other
liabilities. The accuracy of the Company&#146;s assessment of these factors is
inherently uncertain, and the Company&#146;s review and assessment of potential
acquisitions will not reveal all existing or potential problems nor will it
permit the Company to become sufficiently familiar with the properties or
entities to fully assess their deficiencies and capabilities. Even when problems
are identified, the other party may be unwilling or unable to provide effective
contractual protection against all or part of the problems. Furthermore, the
Company may not be entitled to contractual indemnification for certain
liabilities, or it may acquire the properties on an &#147;as is, where is&#148; basis.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Dispositions of portions
of the Company&#146;s existing business or properties would be intended to result in
the realization of immediate value but would consequently result in lower cash
flows over the longer term, unless the proceeds are reinvested in more productive
assets.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s reserve data are estimates.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">No one can measure underground accumulations of oil
and natural gas in an exact way. Projecting future production rates and the
timing and amount of development expenditures is also an uncertain process.
Accuracy of reserve estimates depends on the quality of available data and on
economic, engineering and geological interpretation and judgment. As a result,
reserve estimates often differ from the quantities of oil and natural gas
ultimately recovered. To estimate economically recoverable reserves, various
assumptions are made regarding future oil and natural gas prices, production
levels and operating and development costs that may prove incorrect. Any
significant variance from those assumptions could greatly affect estimates of
economically recoverable reserves and future net revenues.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">It should not be assumed
that the present value of future net cash flows from the Company&#146;s proven
reserves is the current value of the estimated natural gas and oil reserves.
Estimates of discounted future net cash flows from proven reserves are based on
prices and costs on the date of the estimate. Actual future prices and costs
may differ materially from those used in net present value estimates, and
future net present value estimates using then-current prices and costs may be
significantly less than current estimates.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company faces significant competition and is
smaller than many of its competitors.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The oil and gas industry
is highly competitive. The Company competes with major and independent oil and
natural gas companies for property acquisitions and for the equipment and labor
required to operate and develop properties. Many of the Company&#146;s competitors have
substantially greater financial and other resources. As a result, those
competitors may be better able to withstand sustained periods of unsuccessful
drilling. In addition, larger competitors may be able to absorb the burden of
any changes in applicable laws and regulations more easily than the Company
can, which would adversely affect the </font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Company&#146;s

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s competitors may use superior technology.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s industry is

future may become obsolete, and the Company may be adversely affected.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company and its subsidiaries
are subject to extensive domestic and foreign laws and regulations on taxation,
exploration and development, and environmental and safety matters in countries
where it owns or operates properties. These laws and regulations are under
continuing review for amendment or expansion, and the Company could be forced
to expend significant resources to comply with new laws or regulations or
changes to existing requirements. Many laws and regulations require drilling
permits and govern the spacing of wells, the prevention of waste, rates of
production and other matters. These statutes and regulations, and any others
that are passed by the jurisdictions where the Company has production could
limit the total number of wells drilled or the total allowable production from
successful wells, which could limit revenues. Noncompliance with these statutes
or failure to establish exemptions from regulations could also result in
substantial penalties, require the posting of substantial surety bonds, or in
the suspension or termination of the Company&#146;s operations.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is subject to various environmental

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company could

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>damage

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Environmental discharges
may move through soil to water supplies or adjoining properties, giving rise to
additional liabilities. Some laws and regulations could impose liability for
failure to notify the proper authorities of a discharge and other failures to
comply with those laws. Environmental laws may also affect the Company&#146;s costs
to acquire properties. The Company does not believe that its environmental
risks are materially different from those of comparable companies in the oil
and gas industry. However, there is no assurance that environmental laws will
not, in the future, result in decreased production, substantially increased
operational costs or other adverse effects to the Company&#146;s combined operations
and financial condition. Pollution and similar environmental risks generally
are not fully insurable.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Derivative instruments expose the Company to risks of
financial loss in a variety of circumstances.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company uses
derivative instruments in an effort to reduce its exposure to fluctuations in
the prices of oil and natural gas. The Company&#146;s derivative instruments expose
it to risks of financial loss in a variety of circumstances, including when:</font></p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>a
counterparty to the Company&#146;s derivative instruments is unable to satisfy its
obligations;</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>production
is delayed or less than expected; or</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>there
is an adverse change in the expected differential between the underlying price
in the derivative instrument and actual prices received for the Company&#146;s
production.</p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Derivative instruments also may limit the Company&#146;s
ability to realize increased revenue from increases in the prices for oil and
natural gas.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company follows the
provisions of Statement of Financial Accounting Standards No.&nbsp;133, &#147;Accounting
for Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities,&#148; which generally requires
the Company to record each hedging transaction as an asset or liability
measured at its fair value. Each quarter, the Company must record changes in
the fair value of its hedges, which could result in significant fluctuations in
net income and stockholders&#146; equity from period to period.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is subject to restrictive debt covenants.</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Covenants in the credit
facility and the indentures governing the Company&#146;s senior subordinated notes
impose significant operating and financial restrictions on it, including the maintenance
of specified financial ratios. These restrictions may adversely affect the
Company&#146;s ability to finance its future operations and capital needs, to react
to changes in its business or industry or to pursue available business
opportunities. If certain events of default occurred under these debt
instruments, the Company&#146;s outstanding indebtedness thereunder may be
accelerated, and its assets may not be sufficient to repay such indebtedness.
Moreover, any new indebtedness that the Company incurs may impose similar or
more restrictive covenants on the Company.</font></p>

<p style="font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 47.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-47.0pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">ITEM 1B.&nbsp;&nbsp; <i>Unresolved Staff Comments.</i><a name="Item1b_UnresolvedStaffComments__073119"></a></font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">None.</font></p>

<p style="font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 47.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-47.0pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">ITEM 2.&nbsp;&nbsp; <i>Properties.</i><a name="Item2_Properties__073126"></a></font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The information appearing
in Item 1 of this Annual Report is incorporated herein by reference.</font></p>

<p style="font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 47.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-47.0pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">ITEM 3.&nbsp;&nbsp; <i>Legal Proceedings.</i><a name="Item3_LegalProceedings__073133"></a></font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is a party to
various legal proceedings consisting of routine litigation incidental to its
businesses, but believes that any potential liabilities resulting from these
proceedings are adequately </font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">covered
by insurance or are otherwise not material. See &#147;Business&#151;Government

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 47.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-47.0pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">ITEM 4.</font></b><font face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp; </font><i>Submission of Matters to a Vote of Security Holders.</i><a name="Item4_SubmissionOfMattersToAVoteO_073138"></a></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Mr.&nbsp;Van Wagenen, who joined the Company in 1979,
has served in his current position since 1991. Prior to assuming their present
positions with the Company, the business experience of each of the other
executive officers for at least the last five years was as follows: Mr.&nbsp;Brunner,
who joined the Company in 1994, served as Vice President&#151;Operations from
1997&nbsp;- 2002; Mr.&nbsp;Cooper, who joined the Company in 1979, served as
Senior Vice President and Western Division Manager from 1998&nbsp;- 2002; Mr.&nbsp;McCoy,
who joined the Company in 1978, served as Senior Vice President from
1998&nbsp;- 2002 and has served as Chief Administrative Officer since 1989; Mr.&nbsp;Beathard,
who joined the Company in 1982, served as Vice President&#151;Engineering from
1997&nbsp;- 2002; Mr.&nbsp;Killelea who joined the Company in 2000, served as
Vice President from 2001&nbsp;- 2005, and has served as Corporate Secretary and
General Counsel since 2004 and 2000, respectively; Mr.&nbsp;Ulm, who joined the
Company in 1999, served as Vice President from 1999&nbsp;- 2002, and has served
as Chief Financial Officer since 1999; and Mr.&nbsp;Marlowe, who joined the
Company in 1991, served as Controller from 1999 - 2004, and has served as Vice
President&#151;Accounting since 2004.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As of February&nbsp;1,
2007, there were 1,946 holders of record of the Company&#146;s Common Stock.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In 2005, the Company paid
four quarterly dividends of $0.0625 per share on its Common Stock. On January&nbsp;24,
2006, the Company&#146;s quarterly dividend was increased by 20% to $0.075 per share
on its Common Stock and the Company paid four quarterly dividends of that
amount during 2006. The declaration and payment of future dividends, and the
amount of such dividends, will depend upon, among other things, the Company&#146;s
future earnings and financial condition, liquidity and capital requirements,
the general economic and regulatory climate and other factors deemed relevant
by the Company&#146;s Board of Directors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s revolving
credit facility (the &#147;Facility&#148;), under which the Company has borrowed funds,
and the Indentures relating to the Company&#146;s 8.250% Senior Subordinated Notes
due 2011 (the &#147;2011 Notes&#148;), 7.875% Senior Subordinated Notes due 2013 (the &#147;2013
Notes&#148;), 6.625% Senior Subordinated Notes due 2015 (the &#147;2015 Notes&#148;) and
6.875% Senior Subordinated Notes due 2017 (the &#147;2017 Notes&#148;) contain covenants
that may restrict the ability of the Company to pay future dividends on the
Company&#146;s Common Stock. For further discussion of the covenants, see &#147;Note 4,
Long Term Debt&#148; to the Consolidated Financial Statements in this report. The
Company does not believe that any of these agreements will restrict the Company&#146;s
ability to pay dividends on its Common Stock in the reasonably foreseeable
future.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">No equity securities of
the Company not registered under the Securities Act of 1933 were sold by the
Company during the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2006.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 15.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During the fourth quarter
of the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2006, no equity securities of the Company
of any class registered by the Company pursuant to Section&nbsp;12 of the Securities
Exchange Act of 1934 were purchased by or on behalf of the Company or any &#147;affiliated
purchaser&#148; of the Company, as defined in Rule&nbsp;10b-18(a)(3)&nbsp;under
the Securities Exchange Act.</font></p>

<p style="font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 47.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-47.0pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">ITEM 7.&nbsp;&nbsp; <i>Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results
of Operations</i><a name="Item7_ManagementsDiscussionAndAna_084544"></a></font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Statements in the following discussion may be
forward-looking and involve risks and uncertainties. The Company&#146;s financial
results are most directly affected by changing prices for its production.
Changing prices can influence not only current results of operations but the
determination of the Company&#146;s proved reserves and available sources of
financing, including the determination of the borrowing base under its bank
credit facility. The Company&#146;s results depend not only on hydrocarbon prices
generally, but on its ability to market its production on favorable terms. &#160;On a longer term basis, the Company&#146;s
financial condition and results of operations are affected by its ability to
replace reserves as they are produced through successful exploration,
development and acquisition activities. The Company&#146;s results could also be
adversely affected by adverse regulatory developments and operational risks
associated with oil and gas operations. For further discussion of risks and
uncertainties that may affect the Company&#146;s results, see &#147;Item 1A&#151;Risk Factors&#148;
and the discussion below.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The following discussion
of the Company&#146;s financial condition and results of operations reflects the
recasting as discontinued operations of the Company&#146;s Thailand and Hungary
operations for all periods presented prior to 2006. See Note 11&#151;&#147;Discontinued Operations&#148;
to the Consolidated Financial Statements in &#147;Item 8&#151;Financial Statements and
Supplementary Data&#148;. Except where noted, the following discussion relates to
the Company&#146;s continuing activities only. However, the assets comprising the
Company&#146;s continuing operations have changed substantially during the periods
presented, which affects comparability between periods. The Company acquired
Northrock on September&nbsp;27, 2005 and Latigo on May&nbsp;2, 2006, and
disposed of 50% of its interests in its Gulf of Mexico properties on May&nbsp;31,
2006. For summary pro forma results of operations from the Company&#146;s continuing
operations as if the Northrock and Latigo acquisitions had occurred on January&nbsp;1,
2004, please refer to Note 5&#151;&#147;Acquisitions&#148; to the Consolidated Financial
Statements in &#147;Item 8&#151;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&#148;.</font></p>

<p style="font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Executive Overview<a name="ExecutiveOverview_084554"></a></font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s objective is to explore for, develop,
acquire and produce oil and gas in select locations. In pursuit of that
objective, the Company&#146;s goal for each year is to add more oil and gas reserves
than it produces. The year 2006 marked the fifteenth consecutive year of
reserve replacement for the Company.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company pursues a balanced approach in core areas
located in major oil and gas provinces in the United States and internationally.
The Company follows a strict set of criteria when selecting areas of the world
in which to explore. Areas selected are viewed as having proven oil and gas
resources, having reasonable economic terms and possessing low political risk.
Following these criteria, the Company operates internationally in onshore
Canada and also conducts exploration activities in offshore New Zealand and
Vietnam. The Company also seeks to maintain a balanced mixture of the gas/oil
ratio of its proven reserves base. Over the last several years, the Company has
transitioned from a predominately offshore focused company to a company with
the majority of its reserves located in the onshore regions of North America.
As of December&nbsp;31, 2006, approximately 94% of the Company&#146;s reserves are
located onshore. As a result of this transition, the Company has lengthened its
reserves to production index to over 12 years.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At the end of 2006, proven reserves reached 2,213 Bcfe
and production for the year averaged more than 83,500 BOE per day (501,000 Mcfe
per day). Oil and gas pricing and production volumes are important components
of an exploration and development company&#146;s growth in net income and cash flow.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Oil and gas capital and
exploration cash expenditures for 2006 were approximately $1.7 billion.
Exploration and development operations were allocated approximately $943
million, and approximately $787 million was spent on selective acquisitions in
the Company&#146;s core areas of operations. For 2006 the </font></p>


 <p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:24.0pt 0pt .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font face="Times New Roman">38</font></p> <br><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="center">

<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='38',FILE='C:\fc\60102340993_H10771_1796423\5322-1-dm.htm',USER='jmsproofassembler',CD='Mar  1 10:25 2007' -->
<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">



<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Company
drilled 488 wells with 432 successfully completed, an 89% success rate. During
2006, approximately 497 Bcfe of proven reserves were added to the Company&#146;s
reserves ledger.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">2006 Results</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Total revenue for 2006 was
$1,745.0 million and net income totaled $446.2&nbsp;million, or $7.74 per share.
Cash flow from operations totaled $651.9 million. As of December&nbsp;31, 2006,
long-term debt was $2,319.7 million, increasing from December&nbsp;31, 2005 by
$676.2&nbsp;million. The Company&#146;s debt to total capitalization ratio, an
indicator of a company&#146;s financial strength, was 47% at December&nbsp;31, 2006
and cash and cash equivalents decreased from $57.7&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31,
2005 to approximately $22.7 million at December&nbsp;31, 2006. The increase in
debt and the decrease in cash are both due primarily to&nbsp;the closing of the
Latigo acquisition and increased capital expenditures.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Strategic
Alternatives Process</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On February&nbsp;15, 2007,
the Company confirmed that its Board of Directors previously initiated the
exploration of a range of strategic alternatives to enhance shareholder value
and is continuing to do so, including the possible sale or merger of Pogo, the
sale of its Canadian, Gulf Coast, Gulf of Mexico or other significant assets,
and changes to the Company&#146;s business plan. Pogo has retained Goldman, Sachs&nbsp;&amp;
Co. and TD Securities Inc. as financial advisors for the process.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Acquisition of
Latigo Petroleum Inc.</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On May&nbsp;2, 2006, the
Company completed the acquisition of Latigo Petroleum,&nbsp;Inc. (&#147;Latigo&#148;), a
privately held exploration and production company for approximately $764.9
million. The purchase price was funded using cash on hand and debt financing. As
of December&nbsp;31, 2006, Latigo&#146;s estimated proved reserves were
approximately 328 Bcfe. Latigo&#146;s operations are concentrated in the Permian
Basin and Panhandle of Texas.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Sale of 50% of Gulf
of Mexico Interests</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On May&nbsp;31, 2006, the
Company closed the sale of an undivided 50 percent interest of each of its Gulf
of Mexico oil and gas leasehold interests and related pipelines and equipment
to an affiliate of Mitsui&nbsp;&amp; Co., Ltd., for approximately $448.8
million. The proceeds were used to repay a portion of the debt used to finance
the Latigo acquisition. As of December&nbsp;31, 2005, the interests sold were
attributed approximately 143 Bcfe of net estimated proven oil and gas reserves.
The Company recognized a pre-tax gain of $302.7 million related to the sale in
the second quarter of 2006.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Issuance of Senior
Subordinated Notes</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On June&nbsp;6, 2006, the
Company issued and sold $450 million aggregate principal amount of 7.875%
Senior Subordinated Notes due 2013 (the &#147;2013 Notes&#148;). Net proceeds were used
to reduce outstanding debt under the Company&#146;s credit facility.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Recognition of
Income Tax Benefit</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During 2006, the Company&#146;s
consolidated effective tax rate was 10.6%, down from 36.7% in 2005. &#160;This decrease relates to the enactment of a
reduction of the Alberta and Saskatchewan provincial tax rates, in addition to
a reduction in the statutory Canadian federal income tax rate, which generated
a one-time deferred tax benefit of approximately $112 million.</font></p>


 <p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:24.0pt 0pt .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font face="Times New Roman">39</font></p> <br><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="center">

<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='39',FILE='C:\fc\60102340993_H10771_1796423\5322-1-dm.htm',USER='jmsproofassembler',CD='Mar  1 10:25 2007' -->
<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">



<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Commodity Derivatives</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Although the Company&#146;s
collars are effective as economic hedges, the sale of 50% of the Company&#146;s Gulf
of Mexico interests on May&nbsp;31, 2006 and the forecasted shut-in hydrocarbon
production from the Company&#146;s Gulf of Mexico properties (resulting primarily
from hurricane activity during the third quarter of 2005) caused certain of the
gas and crude oil collar contracts to lose their qualification for hedge
accounting. The Company recognized a $7.3 million non-cash gain related to
these contracts in 2006.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">2007 Capital Budget</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company has
established a $720 million exploration and development budget (excluding
property acquisitions) for 2007. The Company expects to spend approximately
$199 million on exploration and $521 million on development activities. The
capital budget calls for the drilling of approximately 370 wells during 2007,
including wells in the United States, Canada, and New Zealand.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">2007 Production
Outlook Update</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company provided 2007
production guidance in its Form 8-K dated February&nbsp;15, 2007. These
estimates are subject to change, and actual results could differ materially,
depending upon the amount of Gulf of Mexico production that remains shut-in,
the timing of any such production coming back on-line, the availability of
oilfield services, acquisitions, divestitures and many other factors that are
beyond the Company&#146;s control. Please read &#147;Forward-Looking Statements.&#148;</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Exposure to Oil and
Gas Prices and Availability of Oilfield Services</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Oil and natural gas prices
have historically been seasonal, cyclical and volatile. Prices depend on many
factors that the Company cannot control such as weather and economic, political
and regulatory conditions. The average prices the Company is currently
receiving for production are higher than historical average prices. A future
drop in oil and gas prices could have a serious adverse effect on cash flow and
profitability. Sustained periods of low prices could have a serious adverse
effect on the Company&#146;s operations and financial condition. Additionally, the
cost of drilling, completing and operating wells and installing facilities and
pipelines is often uncertain and have each increased substantially. The market
for oil field services is currently very competitive and shortages or delays in
delivery or availability of equipment or fabrication yards could impact the
Company&#146;s ability to conduct oil and gas drilling and completion operations.</font></p>

<p style="font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 10.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Results of
Operations<a name="ResultsOfOperations_141554"></a></font></b></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Oil and Gas
Revenues</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s oil and gas revenues for 2006 were
$1,375.4 million, an increase of approximately 13% from oil and gas revenues of
$1,216.2 million for 2005, which were an increase of approximately 25% from oil
and gas revenues of $973.1 million for 2004. The following table reflects an
analysis of variances in the Company&#146;s oil and gas revenues (expressed in
millions) between years:</font></p>

<p style="line-height:1.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;"><font size="1" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The increase in the Company&#146;s oil and gas revenues in
2006, compared to 2005, is related to increases in both the average price that
the Company received for its oil and condensate production volumes and an
increase in the Company&#146;s hydrocarbon production volumes, partially offset by a
decrease in the average price that the Company received for its natural gas
production volumes. The increase in the Company&#146;s oil and gas revenues in 2005,
compared to 2004, is related to increases in both the average price that the
Company received for its hydrocarbon production volumes and an increase in the
Company&#146;s natural gas production volumes, partially offset by a decrease in
crude oil and condensate production volumes. The increase in oil and gas revenues
for 2006, compared to 2005 and for 2005 compared to 2004, was also the result
of an increase in NGL production volumes and in the average price that the
Company received for those volumes.</font></p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 20.0pt;text-indent:-20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(a)</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>Average prices for the
United States reflect the impact of the Company&#146;s price hedging activity. Price
hedging activity reduced the average price per Mcf. of the Company&#146;s United
States natural gas production $0.03 and $0.11 during 2006 and 2005,
respectively. The Company had no price hedging activity related to 2004 production.</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 20.0pt;text-indent:-20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(b)</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>Average prices for the
United States include the impact of the Company&#146;s price hedging activity. Price
hedging activity reduced the average price per Bbl of the Company&#146;s crude oil
and condensate production $0.01 and $0.20 during 2006 and 2005, respectively. The
Company had no price hedging activity related to 2004 production. &#160;For average prices, sales volumes equate to
actual production.</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 20.0pt;text-indent:-20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(c)</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font>Northrock Resources was
acquired by the Company on September&nbsp;27, 2005. The average daily
production volumes for Canada in 2005 are presented on an annualized basis,
calculated by dividing the production for the 96 day period that the Company
owned Northrock by 365 days. This presentation is intended to reflect the
impact of the acquisition and is not considered meaningful for comparison
purposes. On a non-annualized basis, the average daily production for the 96
day period was 70.7 MMcf of natural gas and 12,921 bbls of crude oil and
condensate.</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font style="font-style:italic;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Natural
Gas Production.</font></i></font>&nbsp;&nbsp; The
increase in the Company&#146;s natural gas production during 2006, compared to 2005,
was primarily due to the acquisitions of Northrock on September&nbsp;27, 2005
(which only made a partial year contribution to 2005 production) and Latigo on May&nbsp;2,
2006. The increased natural gas production from both of the acquisitions was
partially offset by decreased production in the Company&#146;s </p>


 <p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:24.0pt 0pt .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font face="Times New Roman">42</font></p> <br><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="center">

<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='42',FILE='C:\fc\60102340993_H10771_1796423\5322-1-dm.htm',USER='jmsproofassembler',CD='Mar  1 10:25 2007' -->
<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">



<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Gulf of Mexico region
resulting from the sale of 50% of the Company&#146;s interest in its Gulf of Mexico
properties on May&nbsp;31, 2006, natural production declines, and the curtailment
of production in 2006 due to the infrastructure damage caused by Hurricanes
Katrina and Rita in the third quarter of 2005. The increase in the Company&#146;s
natural gas production during 2005, compared to 2004, was primarily related to
the addition of production from acquisitions made during late 2005 and late
2004, partially offset by shut-in offshore production caused by Hurricanes
Ivan, Katrina and Rita and, to a lesser extent, natural production declines.</font></p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font style="font-style:italic;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Crude
Oil and Condensate Production.</font></i></font><i>&nbsp;&nbsp; </i>The increase in the Company&#146;s crude
oil and condensate production during 2006, compared to 2005, was primarily due
to the Northrock and Latigo acquisitions, partially offset by the Gulf of
Mexico sale, natural production declines, and curtailment of production
resulting from hurricanes. The decrease in the Company&#146;s crude oil and
condensate production during 2005, compared to 2004, resulted primarily from
the shut-in of Gulf of Mexico platforms due to the effects of Hurricanes Ivan,
Katrina and Rita (including Main Pass Block 61/62) during 2005 and, to a lesser
extent, natural production declines. This decrease was partially offset by the
addition of production from the Northrock acquisition made on September&nbsp;27,
2005.</p>

<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font style="font-style:italic;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">NGL Revenues.</font></i></font><i>&nbsp;&nbsp; </i>The Company&#146;s oil and gas revenues,
and its total liquid hydrocarbon production, reflect the production and sale by
the Company of NGL, which are liquid products that are extracted from natural
gas production. The increase in NGL revenues for 2006, compared with 2005,
related to an increase in the average price that the Company received for its
NGL production to $37.71 in 2006 from $34.56 in 2005 and an increase in NGL
production volumes. The increase in NGL revenues for 2005, compared with 2004,
related to an increase in the average price that the Company received for its
NGL production to $34.56 in 2005 from $28.09 in 2004 and an increase in NGL
production volumes.</p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Gain (loss) on Sale
of Assets</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Gain (loss) on the sale of
assets is derived from the sale of oil and gas properties and other assets,
including tubular stock and vehicles. On May&nbsp;31, 2006, the Company sold an
undivided 50 percent interest in each and all of its Gulf of Mexico oil and gas
leasehold interests and related pipelines and equipment to an affiliate of
Mitsui&nbsp;&amp; Co., Ltd., for approximately $448.8 million, after purchase
price adjustments. The sale resulted in a pre-tax gain of $302.7 million. This
gain, along with $2 million of pre-tax gains on sales of other properties and
assets, has been reflected in the caption &#147;Gain (loss) on sale of properties&#148;
in the Company&#146;s results of operations.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Other Revenues</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Other revenue is derived
from sources other than the current production of hydrocarbons. This revenue
includes, among other items: natural gas inventory sales, pipeline imbalance
settlements and revenue from salt water disposal activities. The increase in
the Company&#146;s other revenues in 2006, compared to 2005 and 2004, is related
primarily to $59.1 million of natural gas inventory sales from the Company&#146;s
Canadian operations for 2006. Only $5.6 million of these gas inventory sales
were made in 2005 in the period subsequent to the Company&#146;s acquisition of
Northrock on September&nbsp;27, 2005. Gas inventory sales are related solely to
the Company&#146;s Canadian operations and were therefore not present in 2004.</font></p>

<p style="line-height:1.0pt;margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;"><font size="1" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Lease Operating
Expenses</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The increase in lease operating expenses for 2006,
compared to 2005, is primarily related the inclusion of a full year of expenses
for Northrock, which was acquired in late September&nbsp;2005; the acquisition
of Latigo in May&nbsp;2006; higher costs being charged by service companies in
2006 relative to 2005; and, to a lesser extent, costs associated with hurricane
related repairs. These higher expenses were only partially offset by the
reduction in lease operating expense related to the sale of 50% of the Company&#146;s
Gulf of Mexico offshore interests on May&nbsp;31, 2006. The increase in lease
operating expenses for 2005, compared to 2004, is related primarily to
increased expenses incurred related to onshore properties acquired by the
Company in the fourth quarter of 2004 and throughout 2005, increased
maintenance expenses on several of the Company&#146;s significant offshore
properties due to damage from Hurricanes Ivan, Katrina and Rita (which were
only partially offset by insurance recoveries), and also to higher costs being
charged by service companies in 2005 relative to 2004. The Company currently
expects lease operating expenses to increase in future periods with the
addition of Latigo related expenses for an entire reporting period. This
increase in 2007 should be partially mitigated by the property sales discussed
in &#147;Gain (loss) on sale of assets&#148; above.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On a per unit of
production basis, the Company&#146;s total lease operating expenses were $1.45 per
Mcfe for 2006, $0.98 per Mcfe for 2005 and $0.61 per Mcfe for 2004. The
increased unit costs in 2006 and 2005 were primarily related to the increased
expenses discussed above, compounded by natural production declines and reduced
offshore hydrocarbon production related to hurricane damage.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">General and
Administrative Expenses</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The increase in general and administrative expenses
for 2006, compared with 2005, and 2005 compared with 2004, is primarily related
to increases in the size of the Company&#146;s workforce due to acquisitions,
increased benefit expenses and increases in compensation. The Company currently
expects general and administrative expenses to increase in future periods with
the addition of Latigo related expenses for the entire reporting period and the
establishment of a Change of Control Retention Program to provide retention
incentive for eligible employees during 2007. See Note 7&#151;&#147;Severance and
Retention Incentive Program&#148; to the Consolidated Financial Statements in &#147;Item
8&#151;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&#148; for additional information on
the Change of Control Retention Program.</font></p>


 <p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:24.0pt 0pt .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font face="Times New Roman">44</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">
<div>


<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On a per unit of
production basis, the Company&#146;s general and administrative expenses were $0.71
per Mcfe in 2006, $0.56 per Mcfe in 2005 and $0.38 per Mcfe in 2004. The
increased unit costs resulted from the increases in expenses discussed above.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Exploration Expenses</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Exploration expenses
consist primarily of exploratory geological and geophysical costs that are
expensed as incurred and rental payments required under oil and gas leases to
hold non-producing properties (&#147;delay rentals&#148;). The increase in exploration
expenses for 2006, compared to 2005, resulted primarily from an increase in
seismic activity in the Company&#146;s Canadian and Vietnam operations and an
increase in delay rentals in the Company&#146;s Canadian operation and Gulf Coast
region, partially offset by decreased seismic activity in the New Zealand
operation and a decrease in exploration activity in the Gulf of Mexico due to
the sale of 50% of the Company&#146;s interests. The increase in exploration
expenses for 2005, compared to 2004, resulted primarily from increased seismic
operations in the Company&#146;s New&nbsp;Zealand and Canadian operations, which
were partially offset by decreased 3-D seismic acquisition activities in
the Gulf of Mexico and decreased seismic operations in the Company&#146;s Gulf Coast
region.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Dry Hole and Impairment Expenses</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Dry hole and impairment
expenses relate to costs of unsuccessful exploratory wells drilled and
impairment of oil and gas properties. During 2006, the Company drilled 25 gross
unsuccessful exploratory wells (20.3 net to the Company&#146;s interest) for a total
cost of approximately $60.9 million; in 2005 the Company drilled 9 unsuccessful
exploratory wells (7.1 net to the Company&#146;s interest) for a total cost of $67.1
million; and in 2004 the Company drilled 7 unsuccessful exploratory wells (5.6
net to the Company&#146;s interest) for a total cost of $40.2 million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Generally accepted
accounting principles require that if the expected future cash flow of the
Company&#146;s reserves on a proved property fall below the cost that is recorded on
the Company&#146;s books, these costs must be impaired and written down to the
property&#146;s fair value. Depending on market conditions, including the prices for
oil and natural gas, and the results of operations, a similar test may be
conducted at any time to determine whether impairments are appropriate.
Depending on the results of this test, an impairment could be required on some
of the Company&#146;s proved properties, and this impairment could have a material
negative non-cash impact on the Company&#146;s earnings and balance sheet. Unproved
properties are reviewed quarterly to determine if there has been impairment of
the carrying value, with any such impairment charged to expense in the period. The
evaluation of unproved properties requires management&#146;s judgment to estimate
the fair value of leasehold and exploratory costs related to drilling activity
in a given area. Drilling activities in an area by other companies may also
effectively condemn unproved properties. As a result of its review of proved
and unproved properties, the Company recognized impairments to oil and gas
properties of approximately $45.7 million during 2006, approximately
$20.1&nbsp;million during 2005 and $21.4 million during 2004.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Depreciation, Depletion and Amortization Expenses</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s provision
for DD&amp;A expense is based on its capitalized costs and is determined on a
cost center by cost center basis using the units of production method. The
Company generally establishes cost centers for its onshore oil and gas
activities on the basis of a reasonable aggregation of properties with a common
geologic structural feature or stratigraphic condition. The Company generally
creates cost centers on a field-by-field basis for oil and gas activities in offshore
areas.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The increase in the Company&#146;s
DD&amp;A expense for 2006, compared to 2005, resulted primarily from a decrease
in the percentage of the Company&#146;s production coming from fields that have
DD&amp;A rates that are lower than the Company&#146;s recent historical composite
DD&amp;A rate (principally offshore fields and legacy onshore fields) and a
corresponding increase in the percentage of the Company&#146;s production coming
from fields that have DD&amp;A rates that are higher than the Company&#146;s recent
historical composite </font></p>


 <p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:24.0pt 0pt .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font face="Times New Roman">45</font></p> <br><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="center">

<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='45',FILE='C:\fc\59191230755_H10771_1791319\5322-1-do.htm',USER='jmsproofassembler',CD='Feb 28 19:13 2007' -->
<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">



<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt;text-indent:0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">rate
(principally production from the Northrock and Latigo acquisitions). The
Company currently expects its average DD&amp;A rate to increase during 2007, as
the effects of the higher rate per Mcf Latigo properties and the sale of the
lower rate per Mcf Gulf of Mexico properties have a greater impact on the
Company&#146;s overall production profile.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The increase in the
Company&#146;s DD&amp;A expense for 2005, compared to 2004, resulted primarily from
an increased DD&amp;A rate caused by a decrease in the percentage of the
Company&#146;s production coming from fields that have DD&amp;A rates that are lower
than the Company&#146;s recent historical composite DD&amp;A rate (principally
properties in the Gulf of Mexico which were shut-in due to hurricane downtime)
and a corresponding increase in the percentage of the Company&#146;s production
coming from fields that have DD&amp;A rates that are higher than the Company&#146;s
recent historical composite rate (principally increased production from
properties acquired through corporate acquisitions).</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Production and Other Taxes</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The increase in production
and other taxes for 2006, compared to 2005, and for 2005, compared to 2004, is
primarily related to increased severance taxes due to higher onshore production
volumes and higher crude and condensate prices, partially offset by lower
natural gas prices, and higher ad valorem taxes due to acquisitions.</font></p>

<p style="font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 3.0pt 30.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:-10.0pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Other</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9.0pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-indent:20.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Other

to Company asset retirement obligations under generally accepted accounting
principles, recognition of recoveries from business interruption insurance,
write-down of tubular inventory values and various other operating expenses. The
following table shows the significant items included in Other and the changes
between periods (expressed in millions):</font></p>
